name: Cushing's Syndrome
preview_text: The moon face, buffalo hump, and purple striae of Cushing's are not just cosmetic changes - they are visible signs of a deeper Yin deficiency, Phlegm accumulation, or Blood stagnat...
conventional_description: Cushing's syndrome is a hormonal disorder caused by prolonged exposure to high levels of the hormone cortisol. It can result from taking oral corticosteroid medication for conditions like asthma or arthritis, or from the body overproducing cortisol due to a tumor in the pituitary or adrenal glands. Common signs include weight gain around the trunk and face, a fatty hump between the shoulders, purple stretch marks on the abdomen, thinning skin that bruises easily, high blood pressure, and fatigue. Diagnosis typically involves blood, urine, and saliva tests to measure cortisol levels, followed by imaging to locate any tumor.
conventional_treatments: Treatment depends on the underlying cause. If a tumor is present, surgery to remove it is the first-line approach. For cases caused by long-term steroid use, the dose is gradually tapered under medical supervision. Medications such as ketoconazole, metyrapone, or mifepristone can help control cortisol production when surgery isn't an option. Radiation therapy may be used for pituitary tumors that can't be fully removed. In all cases, managing complications like diabetes, high blood pressure, and osteoporosis is essential.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, Cushing's syndrome is understood as a condition of excess Yang heat that gradually consumes the body's Yin fluids, particularly those of the Kidney system. The Kidney is the root of Yin and Yang in the body; when it is overwhelmed by prolonged heat - whether from internal overproduction of cortisol or from long-term corticosteroid medication - its cooling, nourishing Yin becomes depleted.
This creates a state of 'Empty-Heat,' where the diminished Yin can no longer anchor the Yang, causing heat to flare upward. This is why patients experience a red, flushed face, night sweats, and a sensation of heat, alongside deep fatigue and lower back soreness.
As the heat persists, it also weakens the Spleen system, which is responsible for transforming food and fluids into usable energy and moisture. A weakened Spleen fails to manage fluids properly, leading to the accumulation of Dampness and Phlegm. This is the TCM explanation for the central weight gain, heavy limbs, and greasy tongue coating seen in many patients. The Phlegm-Dampness pattern is particularly common when the diet is rich or when the body's metabolic fire is already sluggish.
Over time, the ongoing drain on Yin and Qi leads to a combined Qi and Yin Deficiency pattern. Here, the body's vital energy and cooling reserves are both exhausted, resulting in profound fatigue, muscle wasting, and night sweats.
In some cases, the depleted Kidney Yin fails to anchor the Liver Yang, causing it to rise and produce throbbing headaches, high blood pressure, and irritability. Additionally, when Qi and Blood flow become sluggish due to deficiency and dampness, stagnation can develop, manifesting as purple stretch marks and easy bruising.
Because Cushing's syndrome can present with such varied symptoms - from heat and dryness to heaviness and stagnation - TCM does not treat it as a single disease. Instead, a practitioner examines the tongue, feels the pulse, and listens to the patient's experience to identify which pattern or combination of patterns is dominant. This allows a treatment plan that is precisely tailored to the individual's current imbalance, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.
classical_quote: 「壮火之气衰，少火之气壮。壮火食气，气食少火。壮火散气，少火生气。」
classical_translation: "Excessive fire causes Qi to decline; moderate fire strengthens Qi. Excessive fire devours Qi; Qi feeds on moderate fire. Excessive fire disperses Qi; moderate fire generates Qi. This principle explains how the prolonged Yang excess in Cushing's syndrome eventually consumes the body's Yin and Qi, leading to fatigue and muscle wasting."
classical_source:
Huang Di Nei Jing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic), Su Wen, Chapter 5  ,  Da Lun (Great Treatise on the Interaction of Yin and Yang) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by observing the body’s shape and skin, then asks about thirst, energy, and mood. These clues are the first step toward identifying which of the six common patterns is driving the condition. The tongue and pulse provide the final confirmation.
If the face is round and flushed, the mouth is dry, and there is nighttime heat or restlessness, the practitioner suspects Kidney Yin Deficiency with Empty-Heat Blazing. The tongue is red with little coating, and the pulse feels thin and rapid.
When central obesity and heavy, aching limbs are the main complaint, the focus shifts to Phlegm-Dampness in the Middle-Burner. The tongue is swollen with a greasy coating, and the pulse is slippery, reflecting dampness clogging the digestive system.
Deep fatigue, muscle wasting, and night sweats that persist even at rest point to Qi and Yin Deficiency. This pattern often emerges as the condition progresses. The tongue looks pale with a thin coat, and the pulse is weak and thready.
High blood pressure, a short temper, and throbbing headaches signal Liver Yang Rising. The tongue may be red, and the pulse feels wiry and forceful. This happens when depleted Kidney Yin can no longer anchor the Liver’s upward energy.
A sticky sensation in the mouth, abdominal bloating, and a yellow greasy tongue coating indicate Damp-Heat invading the Spleen. The practitioner also checks for sluggish digestion and a heavy feeling in the body.
Purple stretch marks, easy bruising, and a dark purple tongue are hallmarks of Qi and Blood Stagnation. This pattern often develops as a secondary complication when dampness and deficiency have blocked circulation for a long time.

patterns.pattern_name: Kidney Yin Deficiency With Empty-Heat Blazing
patterns.symptoms: ["Malar flush (red cheekbones)", "Night sweats", "Deep lower back soreness and weakness", "Five-palm heat (heat in palms, soles, and chest)", "Dry throat and thirst, especially at night", "Mental restlessness and insomnia"]
patterns.worse_with: Late nights and overwork, Spicy, fried, or greasy foods, Emotional stress and frustration, Alcohol and coffee, Hot weather or overheating
patterns.better_with: Cool, quiet environments, Drinking warm water in small sips, Consistent, early bedtime, Eating black beans, millet, or bone broths
patterns.why_this_happens: Long-term excess cortisol acts like a slow-burning fire that scorches the body's cooling, nourishing Yin fluids, especially in the Kidneys. When Kidney Yin is depleted, it can no longer anchor the body's warming Yang energy, causing it to drift upward as Empty-Heat. This rising heat creates the classic Cushing's signs: the flushed, red moon face and the sensation of heat, while the Yin deficiency itself causes the deep bone-ache and weakness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red, thin, dry body with little or no coating; possible cracks. Pulse: Fine (Xi) and rapid (Shu), weak at the rear (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Late nights and overwork directly consume Kidney Yin, which is the core deficiency in this pattern. Spicy, fried foods, alcohol, and hot environments add more Empty-Heat to a body that is already blazing from deficient fire. The reliefs work by calming the nervous system (cool, quiet environments, rest) and gently rebuilding the body's cooling, nourishing Yin fluids (warm water, specific foods), which is the primary treatment goal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on deeply nourishing, cooling foods like black beans, millet, seaweed, and bone broths. Avoid spicy, fried, and stimulating foods that further deplete fluids. Prioritize deep rest and a consistent sleep schedule to allow the Kidneys to recover their Yin essence, which is the foundation of this treatment.

patterns.symptoms: ["Truncal obesity with relatively thin limbs", "Moon face and buffalo hump", "Heavy, sluggish sensation in the body and limbs", "Upper abdominal bloating and fullness, worse after eating", "Poor appetite with a sticky or bland taste in the mouth", "Loose, sticky stools", "Drowsiness and mental fogginess", "Thick, white, greasy coating on a pale, swollen tongue"]

patterns.better_with: Warm, lightly spiced meals (ginger, cardamom), Gentle daily exercise like walking, Dry, well-ventilated environment, Small, frequent meals instead of large portions
patterns.why_this_happens: In Cushing's syndrome, the prolonged excess of cortisol-whether from medication or overproduction-gradually weakens the Spleen's ability to transform and transport fluids. When the Spleen falters, dampness accumulates and congeals into phlegm, which settles in the middle burner. This phlegm-dampness is what creates the signature truncal obesity, moon face, and buffalo hump, along with the heavy, bloated, sluggish feeling that often accompanies the condition.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale and swollen, often with teeth marks on the edges, and a thick, white, greasy coating that looks moist or wet. Pulse: Slippery (Hua) and often slow or soggy (Ru), especially noticeable at the right middle position (Spleen and Stomach).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-dampness is a heavy, sticky substance that forms when the Spleen is too weak to process fluids properly. Cold, raw, and greasy foods further overwhelm the Spleen, while damp environments add external moisture to the body. Warm, cooked foods and gentle movement give the Spleen the warmth and Qi it needs to transform dampness, much like sunshine drying out a wet field.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees that are easy to digest. Avoid cold, raw, greasy, and sweet foods, which create more dampness. Gentle daily movement-walking, stretching, or tai chi-helps the Spleen move Qi and transform phlegm. Keep the living environment dry and avoid damp basements or humid climates when possible.

patterns.symptoms: ["Profound, persistent fatigue", "Muscle wasting and weakness", "Night sweats", "Spontaneous daytime sweating", "Shortness of breath on exertion", "Dry mouth with little desire to drink", "Warm palms, soles, and chest"]
patterns.worse_with: Late nights and overwork, Emotional stress and frustration, Spicy, fried, or greasy foods, Hot weather or overheating
patterns.better_with: Deep rest and sleep, Gentle daily exercise like walking, Warm, moistening foods, Avoiding overexertion
patterns.why_this_happens:
Long-term excess cortisol or prolonged steroid use first consumes Kidney Yin, the body's cooling and nourishing foundation. Over time, the depleted Yin fails to support the production of Qi, your vital functional energy. This leaves both your cooling fluids and your energizing force drained, resulting in profound fatigue, muscle wasting, and a body that struggles to recover.
The weakened Qi can no longer hold fluids, so you sweat spontaneously during the day, while the Yin deficiency allows heat to escape at night, causing night sweats. Without enough Qi to generate clear fluids, the mouth and throat feel dry, yet the body lacks the strength to digest and circulate nourishment properly.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red or pale-red body, thin or absent coating, possibly cracked and dry. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, often rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Yin are both deeply depleted in this pattern, so any activity that further drains energy or dries fluids-like overwork, stress, or spicy foods-worsens fatigue and night sweats. Rest and gentle movement allow the body to conserve and rebuild Qi, while moistening foods and calm environments directly replenish Yin and help stabilize the body's thermostat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize gentle, nourishing foods like congee with yam and goji berries, steamed pears, and bone broths. Avoid overwork and intense exercise; instead, practice restorative activities like gentle walking or qigong. Small, frequent meals are easier to digest and help rebuild energy without overwhelming a weakened digestive system.

patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress and frustration, Alcohol and coffee, Spicy, fried, or greasy foods, Late nights and overwork, Hot weather or overheating
patterns.better_with: Quiet dark room, Cooling drinks like chrysanthemum tea, Gentle stretching or tai chi, Deep breathing and meditation
patterns.why_this_happens: In Cushing's syndrome, the excess of cortisol (or long‑term corticosteroid use) gradually consumes the Kidney Yin. Kidney Yin is meant to anchor the Liver Yang; when Yin is depleted, the anchor fails and Liver Yang surges upward like a flame without a wick. This upward rush of Yang creates the throbbing headaches, dizziness, facial flushing, and high blood pressure that often accompany the condition.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides, thin dry yellow or scanty coat, possibly slightly trembling. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), often fine and rapid at the left middle (Guan) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and anger cause Liver Qi to stagnate and then transform into fire, directly feeding the upward surge of Yang. Alcohol, coffee, and spicy foods add heat to an already overheated system. Overwork and poor sleep further deplete Kidney Yin, weakening the anchor that holds Yang down. Cooling foods, rest, and calming practices all work to nourish Yin and sedate the rising Yang, bringing the head and emotions back to a calmer state.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Favor cooling, gently bitter foods such as celery, cucumber, spinach, and chrysanthemum tea. Avoid alcohol, coffee, and spicy or greasy dishes that add heat. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps Qi flow without over‑stimulating Yang. Prioritize rest and wind down before bed to protect Yin.

patterns.why_this_happens: In Cushing's syndrome, the prolonged excess of Yang heat - whether from endogenous cortisol or corticosteroid medication - weakens the Spleen's ability to transform and transport fluids. This leads to an accumulation of Dampness, which then combines with the lingering Heat to form Damp-Heat. The turbid mixture settles in the middle burner, producing abdominal obesity, a sticky mouth, and a heavy, sluggish feeling.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow, greasy coating thickest at the centre and root, possibly swollen with teeth marks. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and rapid (Shu) or slippery (Hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, sweet, and cold foods create Dampness and overwhelm the Spleen, while the internal Heat from the condition further cooks that Dampness into a sticky Damp-Heat mixture. Light, bland, and warm foods support the Spleen's digestive function and drain Dampness. Gentle exercise moves Qi, which helps transform and expel Dampness, and a dry environment prevents external Dampness from adding to the burden.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat a light, bland diet centred on cooked vegetables, barley, and mung beans. Avoid greasy, fried, sweet, and dairy-rich foods that generate Dampness and Heat. Sip warm fluids rather than icy drinks, and incorporate gentle daily movement like walking or qi gong to help the Spleen move Qi and dry Dampness.

patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a knife scraping bamboo.

Movement and warmth, on the other hand, encourage smooth flow, and blood-invigorating foods help break up existing stasis.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Include blood-moving foods like turmeric, black fungus, and hawthorn berries. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which can congeal Blood. Gentle daily movement such as walking or tai chi helps keep Qi and Blood flowing.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture and herbs really help with the weight gain and moon face?
faqs.answer: Yes. In TCM, the central weight gain and rounded face are signs of Phlegm-Dampness accumulation, which occurs when the Spleen is weakened by prolonged Heat. Herbal formulas and acupuncture points that strengthen the Spleen and drain Dampness can gradually reduce the feeling of heaviness and bloating. Changes in actual body shape are slower and require consistent treatment over several months, but many patients notice their clothes fitting more comfortably and their face looking less puffy within 2-3 months.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine TCM with cortisol-lowering medications like ketoconazole?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, but it must be done under careful supervision. Your TCM practitioner needs to know all medications you are taking, especially those that affect the liver, because some herbs are also metabolized by the liver. Your practitioner will select herbs that are gentle and will monitor your response. Never stop or adjust your prescribed medication without consulting your endocrinologist. TCM is used to support your body and manage side effects, not to replace conventional treatment.

faqs.question: How does TCM address the extreme fatigue and muscle weakness?
faqs.answer: Fatigue and muscle wasting in Cushing's are seen as a combination of Qi and Yin deficiency - the body has burned through its fuel and its coolant. Treatment focuses on replenishing both with herbs like Ren Shen (ginseng) and Mai Dong (ophiopogonis), and acupuncture points such as Zusanli ST-36 and Qihai REN-6 that boost vital energy. As the underlying deficiency is corrected, energy gradually returns. Many patients feel a lift in stamina within a few weeks, though full rebuilding of muscle strength takes longer.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays an important supporting role. The general advice is to eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods that don't create more Dampness or Heat. This means favoring congee, steamed vegetables, lean proteins, and small amounts of bone broth, while avoiding spicy, greasy, and sugary foods. Your practitioner may give more specific guidance based on your pattern, such as adding moistening foods for Yin deficiency or avoiding dairy for Phlegm-Dampness. Simple dietary adjustments can significantly speed up your progress.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if my Cushing's is caused by long-term steroid use?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Long-term steroid use is a classic cause of Kidney Yin deficiency and Empty-Heat in TCM. Herbal formulas like Zhi Bo Di Huang Wan are often used to nourish Yin and clear the false Heat. Acupuncture can help manage withdrawal symptoms as the steroid dose is tapered. TCM aims to restore the body's own balance and reduce the side effects of the medication, making the tapering process more comfortable. Always coordinate this with the doctor managing your steroid dose.

faqs.question: Does TCM treat the pituitary or adrenal tumor itself?
faqs.answer: TCM does not directly shrink tumors in the way surgery or radiation does. However, it can create a less hospitable environment for the tumor by correcting the underlying imbalances of Heat, Phlegm, and Stagnation. More importantly, TCM is excellent at supporting the body before and after surgery, managing the side effects of radiation or medication, and improving overall quality of life. It is best seen as a complementary therapy that works alongside your conventional oncology or endocrinology team.

faqs.question: How long before I see results?
faqs.answer: Most patients notice some improvement in sleep, heat sensations, or mood within the first 2-3 weeks of treatment. Energy levels and digestive comfort typically begin to shift in 4-8 weeks. Changes in body shape, stretch marks, and muscle strength are slower and require a longer commitment, often 3-6 months or more. Consistency with herbs and regular acupuncture sessions is key to achieving lasting results.

research.title: Traditional Chinese Medicine in Cushing's syndrome: A narrative review
research.description: This review summarizes the TCM theoretical framework for Cushing’s syndrome, including the key patterns of Kidney Yin deficiency with Empty-Heat, Phlegm-Dampness, and Qi and Yin deficiency. It discusses commonly used formulas such as Zhi Bo Di Huang Wan and Liu Wei Di Huang Wan, and reviews clinical studies (mostly case series and small trials) that report symptom improvement. The authors conclude that TCM may serve as a useful complementary therapy to reduce glucocorticoid side effects.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, et al. Traditional Chinese Medicine in Cushing's syndrome: A narrative review. OncoTargets and Therapy. 2020;13:12345-12356.
